turns.t: Good morning, Singapore — it's Wednesday, the fourth of November. This is The Meridian Briefing.
Twelve desks. One world. Twenty minutes — let's go.
President Trump says the United States stops four billion dollars a year in military aid to Israel. He said it on television. There is no document.
[curious] A chip company agrees to buy a laser company for a hundred and fifteen billion dollars — and by Tuesday the same deal is worth about seventy-nine.
And Thailand has frozen three and a half million bank accounts. A third of them have no complainant.
[wry] That's a lot of frozen. Where do you want to start?

Israel. Tuesday morning, American midterm election day. Trump phones into Fox News. Phones in. And says he and Prime Minister Netanyahu agreed months ago to end annual American military aid at the end of this year.
His words?
"We were giving them four billion — we are — but it gets cut off at the end of the year." And then: "They don't need it."
[thoughtful] Israel's been the biggest cumulative recipient of American foreign assistance since the Second World War. That's not a small thing to end in a phone call.

It would be the largest change to that relationship in a generation. Which is why how it was said matters as much as what was said. None. No transcript. No readout. No post. The interview is the record. And the actual instrument says something different. It's a ten-year memorandum signed under Obama. Three point eight billion a year, running to September two thousand and twenty-eight. Three point three billion in grant finance for military purchases, five hundred million for joint missile defence. Almost all of it has to be spent with American manufacturers. Most of it does, yes.
And the other side? Has Netanyahu confirmed any of this?

His office declined to comment. The State Department didn't respond. The foreign minister hasn't confirmed it. And Netanyahu is a caretaker. Israel voted on the twenty-seventh of October and produced no majority — his bloc has fifty-three seats, Gadi Eisenkot's has forty-eight.
[pause] So the President announced a deal with a prime minister who currently has no government.
President Herzog begins coalition consultations today. The new Knesset is sworn in on the tenth.
What did Israeli politicians make of it?

The complaint was about the channel, not the policy. Eisenkot — former chief of staff of the army — said the public learned of a strategic shift through the media, and that Netanyahu "can no longer be trusted, and he must be replaced." Yair Golan, who leads The Democrats, said ending the aid would seriously damage Israeli security.
And the sceptical read?
The Times of Israel wrote in its own voice that the claim "appears to almost certainly be false," given the memorandum runs to twenty twenty-eight.
[deadpan] Their own voice. Not a quoted analyst.
Their own voice. And a president can't do it alone — Congress appropriates the money every year. Al Jazeera's White House correspondent called the timing a "November surprise."
What would settle it?
A written notification to Congress. Or a line in the next budget request. Neither exists today.
[sighs] Right. And oil?
Brent fell about three per cent to a hundred and one on the remarks, then recovered to a hundred and three by midday in New York.
Speaking of which — there was a strike.
Five explosions on Qeshm Island, in the Strait of Hormuz, late Monday. American media attributed them to the United States. Central Command said nothing at all.
And then?
Tuesday morning Trump confirmed it himself. "They built an anti-aircraft facility. As soon as it was completed, we hit it last night very nicely." He called it a minor attack.
[curious] Anything from the Iranian side?
The Revolutionary Guard's navy says three tankers caught fire after hitting naval mines. No vessel named. No casualty figure. None of it independently confirmed.
So we print it as a claim.

We print it as a claim. What is confirmed is a death — an Indian sailor aboard a commercial vessel attacked off the Omani coast. That brings the Indian dead in this conflict to twenty-three, fifteen of them seafarers. And one more from the world desk, because it is the largest civilian toll of the week. Russian bombs hit a school at Komyshuvakha in Zaporizhzhia on Monday — a building used every Monday to hand out food.
Hit once?
Hit, and then hit again. Nine more bombs on the shelter where survivors and rescuers had taken cover. By Tuesday evening the regional administration counted thirty-one dead and fifty-eight missing.
What does the United Nations say?

Danielle Bell, who heads its human rights mission in Ukraine: either Russian forces knew aid was being distributed, "or they failed to take the most basic steps to find out." Either way, she says, it appears to have violated the most fundamental principles of humanitarian law.
[exhales] Moscow's account?
Moscow says it struck soldiers.
Okay. The money block. You've been excited about this one all morning.
[amused] I have. A government bond's yield is really two numbers added together.
Explain it like I've just walked in.
What lenders demand for parting with the money. And what they expect inflation to take from them. The American Treasury publishes both — an ordinary ten-year yield, and an inflation-protected one.
And the gap between them is the forecast.

The gap is the market's own forecast of inflation over the next ten years. On Tuesday the ordinary yield closed at four point nine five per cent. The protected one at two point six five. So the forecast is two point three oh.
Fine. And a year ago?
A year ago the ordinary yield was four point one three. The protected one, one point eight two. The forecast — two point three one.
[pause] Wait. So the forecast went down. Over a year in which oil nearly doubled.
In which American petrol rose thirty-four per cent and headline inflation reached three point seven. The bond market put not one basis point of that into long-run inflation.
[gasps] So where did the eighty-two points go?
All of it was the real rate. Eighty-three points of the eighty-two, in fact.
That's more than all of it.
That's more than all of it. The market has priced this war as a tax on growth and a reason for tighter money — not as inflation.
And the Fed agrees?
The Fed held on the twenty-eighth of October, ten votes to two. And here's the thing — both dissenters wanted a rise. Governor Lisa Cook's first dissent since twenty twenty-two.
[thoughtful] Hawks dissenting against a hold. That's unusual.
The Bank of Japan held two days later with one member pressing for higher too.
What does it mean for an ordinary portfolio?

Nothing is working at once. World equities seven per cent below their fifty-two-week high. Global bonds five and a half below theirs. Gold thirty per cent under a January peak. Bitcoin thirty-eight under its own.
And on Tuesday?

Equities and bonds fell together. That's a rates move, not a growth scare — and it's the opposite of the diversification a mixed portfolio is bought for. Explanation, not advice. And one sceptic, from the people with the most skin in it. J.P. Morgan's fixed-income group just raised its fair-value range for the ten-year to four and a half to five and a quarter.
Which at four point nine five leaves…
Thirty basis points of room. By the reckoning of the people who just raised it.
Home. What happened at Changi?
The Manpower Ministry said on Monday it's investigating about forty-five companies at the airport, over roughly two hundred and seventy workers.
Doing what?
Employment Pass holders were found handling baggage. And the ministry's language is specific — the salaries and occupations declared for those pass holders were false.
[curious] The Employment Pass is the professional pass, isn't it?

Professionals and managers. It is not the pass for lifting suitcases, which is why the declarations had to be wrong for the arrangement to work at all. Within a day. SATS emailed staff thanking them for operational support and encouraging them to volunteer for baggage-handling duties — particularly over the Deepavali long weekend.
[laughs] Head office goes to the belt.

Two-and-a-half-hour blocks. A transport allowance, time off in lieu, and fifteen dollars in vouchers. That part comes from an anonymous employee quoted in the press, not from the company. But here's the sceptical reading, and it comes from the ministry's own published rules. The Employment Pass carries no quota and no levy. The S Pass is capped at ten per cent of a services firm's headcount and costs six hundred and fifty dollars a month a head.
And together?
Work permits and S Passes together are capped at thirty-five per cent in services — the tightest ceiling of any sector.
[thoughtful] So if you've used up both…
You have exactly one uncapped, levy-free channel left. And its price of entry is a declared salary.
Which is precisely the thing alleged to have been falsified. Though a false declaration is still a crime.
Whatever the arithmetic. The ministry hasn't said the firms had no lawful choice. Paying the threshold is legal. Hiring locally is legal. They just cost money.
Technology. The hundred-and-fifteen-billion-dollar deal that wasn't.
Marvell Technology signed an agreement on Sunday to buy Lumentum — the American maker of the lasers that carry data between artificial-intelligence computers.
Biggest chip merger of the year?
Of the year. Announced Monday at a headline value of a hundred and fifteen billion. And Marvell is paying no cash.
[curious] All shares?
Four and a half new Marvell shares for every Lumentum share.
Ah. So what the seller actually gets moves with the buyer's share price.

And Marvell's has been falling hard. By Tuesday's close those four and a half shares were worth seven hundred and seventy-three dollars and eighty-seven cents — not the eleven hundred and thirty-two the announcement described. About seventy-nine billion. Not a hundred and fifteen.
[gasps] It shrank by a third while they were announcing it.
And Marvell's own shareholders have taken about sixty-six billion off the company in three sessions. More than half of what it says it's paying.
What about the premium? There's always a premium.
Twenty-three point nine per cent over Lumentum's close on the twenty-eighth of October — which the filing calls the unaffected date.
[skeptical] Unaffected by what?
Bloomberg reported advanced talks that same day.
[laughs] So the unaffected price was already affected.
Marvell fell thirteen per cent the next session and ten the day after. By the time the agreement was signed, the Marvell those shares were priced against had gone.
What's the trade saying?

Two downgrades on Tuesday. Bank of America's Vivek Arya cut his target from four hundred to two twenty-five, writing that a billion dollars of cost cuts "falls short of offsetting about fifty per cent share dilution."
And the other?
TD Cowen, to Hold — citing "our negative view of the transaction itself in terms of structure and timing, rather than the quality of the asset."
So not the asset. The deal.

And one measure of attention. The Reuters report of the year's biggest chip merger drew five points and no comments on Hacker News. The home lab, briefly, because the shape is the same. The free program most people use to run artificial-intelligence models on their own computers accepted a change on Tuesday.
What does it do?
Lets two separate machines work on the same model at the same moment, over a fast network. Filed in September, merged after forty-nine days by an engineer at Nvidia.
And it's fast?
On the author's own pair of machines, reading a long document got about sixty per cent quicker.
[curious] On the author's own pair.

[deadpan] On the author's own pair. Georgi Gerganov, who founded the project, tried it on his two machines and wrote: "On my pair I can't reproduce. Performance is the same as master." He suspects one of his machines is throttled by a power problem. A maintainer could reproduce it — but only with both machines running at full clock.
So the benchmark needs perfect conditions.
And it was merged on two approvals given that day, with the code owner's own review still outstanding.
Right — take my hand. We're going down the rabbit hole.
[sighs] Every morning with this one.
[laughs] What have we got?
Pinball. Specifically, owning a three-hundred-pound machine in your house and choosing an old one.
Why old?

Because of nineteen seventy-seven. Before it, a pinball machine is electromechanical — scoring done by motors, relays and stepper units, sound by physical bells and chimes, and no computer anywhere in the cabinet.
And after?
After, there's a circuit board.
[thoughtful] And that changes what, exactly — repair?

Everything about repair. An electromechanical machine can be understood by a patient adult with a multimeter. Every function is a wire going somewhere visible, and the parts that wear are springs, contacts and coils that are still made. Depends on boards whose chips are out of production. And a machine built this year depends on boards nobody outside the factory can source.
[pause] So the oldest machines are the most repairable.
That inversion is the whole culture of the hobby.
All right, what does a new one cost? I genuinely have no idea.

Stern Pinball, of Elk Grove Village, Illinois, lists thirty-four titles. Its Pokémon machine — announced in February for the franchise's thirtieth anniversary — is six thousand nine hundred and ninety-nine dollars for the Pro.
And the top?
Nine thousand six hundred and ninety-nine for the Premium. Twelve thousand nine hundred and ninety-nine for the Limited Edition — a run of seven hundred and fifty worldwide.
[gasps] Thirteen thousand dollars for a pinball machine.
Jersey Jack sells Sonic and Harry Potter from about ten thousand to fifteen.
And what does the extra buy?
More mechanisms on the playfield that physically move. Different finishes. A number on a plaque.
And the game?

The code is the same. Which brings the sceptic. The out-of-production list on Jersey Jack's own page has a Toy Story Four Limited Edition marked down from twelve thousand to nine thousand nine hundred and ninety-nine.
[laughs] A limited edition on sale.
A limited edition that goes on sale is a limited edition that didn't sell out.
Is there a cheaper way in?

The Pacific Pinball Museum in Alameda, California. More than a hundred machines across five rooms, arranged chronologically from the eighteen-hundreds to the nineteen-seventies — and every one of them set to free play.
For how much?
Twenty-two dollars for an adult. Twelve for a child. Fifty-five for a family of four.
[warmly] That's the whole argument, isn't it.
Four hundred and fifty museum visits for the price of one machine. And somewhere in the first dozen you'd learn which three you actually want.
And here at home?
Nothing we could find. No museum, no collectors' club, no dealer. It's a hobby a Singapore reader is likeliest to meet on holiday.
[thoughtful] And I gather the research didn't go smoothly.

It didn't, and we said so in print. The main forum, the main subreddit and the hobby's own machine database all refused us on the same morning. Not one. Which makes it a thinner page than this desk wants, and the page says that out loud rather than inventing a consensus.
[warmly] Good. Right — culture and the body, quickly.
A documentary topped the American box office for a third weekend. Eleven point four million dollars, from three thousand two hundred and forty-three theatres.
A documentary at number one?
The first that isn't a concert film to do it since two thousand and four. It's about Elizabeth Holmes, directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, and it runs nearly three hours.
Reviews?
Ninety-six per cent, from two hundred and six critics.
[skeptical] And the sceptic?

Across two hundred and six critics the aggregator surfaces no negative excerpt at all. That's a remarkable consensus on a film whose central question is whether a convicted fraudster should have been given a hundred and seventy-four minutes of sympathetic screen time.
Hm. And on the body?
Soy and pea protein shakes build just as much muscle as whey. Five trials, three hundred and seventy-two untrained adults, all measured by scanner.
[curious] So the tub doesn't matter.
The lifting and the day's total protein do the work. Though the sceptic is real — measure muscle synthesis directly and whey wins per gram, until you dose the plant powder up with leucine.
And who's telling us all this?

[wry] That's the finding. The paper is in the sponsoring society's own journal, and that society lists about forty corporate sponsors — firms selling both whey and plant powders. The authors declare no conflicts and are publicly funded. But almost every other voice on this question is selling you a tub.
One more before the close?
Two quick ones. Apple's new small tablet reaches Singapore on Friday from nine hundred and ninety-nine dollars — and the chip is different depending on how much storage you buy.
[curious] Different how?
The cheaper two get five processor cores and one unit for running artificial-intelligence models on the device. The largest gets six cores and two.
And they say this where?
In a table. Nowhere in the marketing. And the specification page never states the screen's refresh rate at all.
And the watch?
H. Moser limited a new chronograph to a hundred pieces. The caseback is engraved "limited one hundred pieces." The maker's own product page doesn't mention the limitation at all.
[deadpan] The thing the price rests on.
The thing the price rests on. Thailand. In Thai, a money mule is a horse — banchee ma, the horse account. The animal that carries somebody else's load.
And what's new?
Thais have started using it about themselves. On the country's main public forum people write sentences like: "the bank told me I'm a light-brown horse account."
[pause] A risk code has become an identity.
There are five colours, and since last December they're black-letter law. Black, dark-grey, light-grey — and beneath them two brown tiers, where the bank merely found your behaviour odd.
What's the difference between dark and light grey?
Dark grey means a victim has filed a report. Light grey means no complaint has been filed at all.
And how many people are in the no-complaint tiers?
The central bank's own published answers put the light-grey and brown tiers together at about a third of the total.
And the total is?
Three and a half million accounts suspended. Two hundred and forty-six thousand names.
[exhales] And it works?
On the measure it chose, spectacularly. Victim losses fell about seventy-nine per cent from the peak in twenty twenty-four.
So why are we running it?
Because of the design underneath. An amendment last April makes a bank co-liable for a victim's loss unless it can prove it met the standards.
[drawn out] So under-freezing costs the bank money.
And over-freezing costs it nothing. There's no court to which the freeze itself can be taken.
[thoughtful] Then mass over-freezing isn't a bug.

It's the equilibrium the design was built to produce. And the burden is inverted — to clear the lightest listing you must appear in person at a branch and prove a negative. If you succeed, they may reopen that one account.
Who does it fall on?

Market traders. Riders. Resellers. The recently banked — the people the cashless build-out was celebrated for bringing in. A durian seller in Khon Kaen had a hundred and sixty thousand baht frozen because sixteen thousand arrived from a suspected horse account. She got it back about eighteen hours after her Facebook post was shared nearly twenty thousand times. Her words, as reported: "It isn't enough that earning the money exhausts you — now you have to be exhausted over the money you already earned."
And has anyone in Thailand pushed back?
A senate committee, in September last year. Its chair called the practice "improper performance of official duty," and put the legal objection plainly: not freeze first and investigate afterwards.
Is there a precedent for where this goes?
Japan. Eighteen years of it. They criminalised the sale of bank accounts in two thousand and eight and raised the penalty in twenty eleven.
And supply fell?
Supply tripled. By twenty twenty-four arrests for account trading were about three and a half times the twenty eleven level.
[curious] And the fraud itself?

Hit a record. Japan's special-fraud losses nearly doubled in a single year, to a hundred and forty-two billion yen. In January the police panel concluded deterrence is still insufficient — and recommended raising the penalties again.
[pause] So the ratchet just keeps turning.

Which is the argument. The seventy-nine per cent fall measures what victims transferred — not what criminals earned. Money that leaves in one hop into a licensed exchange, or through a company account, or in banknotes that never come back to a bank, never enters that series at all.
[thoughtful] So the fraud may have moved off the measured surface.
Rather than out of the economy. And it was bought with a quarter of a million people who can no longer get paid.
And the rails are generic.

They work beautifully on scam money. They'll work exactly as well on whatever the next list-maker decides to name. A transfer of a hundred and forty baht froze a delivery rider's account for five months — against two hundred and forty-six thousand names on a list no judge has ever seen. That's the Briefing. The full book is on your dashboard — twenty-four pages, footnotes and all.
Read the footnotes. See you tomorrow, Singapore.
